text:
Every line between two tables ends on a row. So how do you say WHICH row? Two customers named Taylor Kim, both in Portland. An order for coffee beans says Taylor Kim. Which one? With no key, Postgres can't tell. It'll store the same row twice. A primary key fixes that: customer one oh one, and customer one oh two.

And Postgres holds a key to two rules: unique, and never null. Customer one is Ada. Add Grace as customer one too, and it's refused. Key one already exists. Leave the ID off? Refused again. No pointer can mean maybe this one, maybe that one.

A key can be two columns. In a roster, student seven takes two courses, and course forty-two has two students. Neither ID is unique, but the pair is: seven in forty-two, only once. And a key should almost never change, because other tables point at it. So what should a key be?

A natural key is a value the thing already has, like a country code. See J P, and you know it's Japan. A surrogate key is a number the database makes up, just to name the row. It means nothing... on purpose.

Why bother? In nineteen thirty-eight, a wallet maker in Lockport, New York, put a sample Social Security card in every wallet. It carried a real person's number, and buyers adopted it. By nineteen forty-three, over five thousand people were using it. One unique number, shared by thousands, and the permanent one got cancelled. A natural key bets on promises you don't control.

It goes wrong quietly, too. Make email the key, and when Ada changes hers, Postgres refuses: her order still points at the old one. Make her user ten instead, and the change just goes through. Keep email unique, just not the key. So a key names a row. Now, let's point at one.
